utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it -- how long is this one? We can admit it in its entirety or only this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's a witness statement that he gave in 2009, I believe, to the RS MUP so yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Exactly. His statement is very short. It's more cover pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3047, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA ANDRIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, that concludes your evidence. I would like to thank you on behalf of this Chamber for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one small piece of administration if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. File. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning. There were two exhibits that were MFI'd pending English translation. I'm referring to P5975 and P6149. And I just wanted to alert the Chamber that English translations are now available and uploaded, and so I would move to have those admitted as full exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has been checking whether certain exhibit was marked for identification only because of lack of English translation or otherwise, but this time based upon the position of the Defence we'll admit it in full -- them, both of them in their entirety. Thank you, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trisic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Trisic, I must draw your attention to a particular Rule of Procedure and Evidence we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any case -- against you for any offence, save and except for the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Trisic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we ask you to speak up a little bit and come closer to the microphones. I would also like you and me to speak our sentences out slowly and to make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide my Defence team with a statement?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D7814 in e-court now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, do you see the statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And have you read and signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I did read it, but I don't see the signature yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I did sign this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today that were put to you then, would your answers in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I would not change anything. They would be the same in essence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the statement and the accompanying documents pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, the two associated exhibits are noted -- it isn't noted there, but I don't find them on our 65 ter list in my own checking. So I would ask that they be allowed to be added. I don't believe they were there because the witness was interviewed after that list was submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the statement as well as two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 92 ter statement will be Exhibit D3048, and the two other documents would be Exhibits D3049 and D3050 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read the summary of Bozidar Trisic's statement in English. [In English] Bozidar Trisic lived in Zaklopaca, and before the war he worked as a teacher in the local primary school. He lived in an ethnically mixed village where the relations between all residents were good. However, after the multi-party elections people began to mistrust one another because of the propaganda, but still there were no incidents in the village to be caused by -- due to the ethnicity. At the beginning of May 1992 two buses carrying around 200 people arrived in Zaklopaca. These people were Muslim inhabitants of local villages who had fled as the Muslim forces wished to mobilise them. Temporary accommodation was found in the village for these people. The new arrivals informed the villagers of Zaklopaca that Muslims had placed barricades at the entrance into the bauxite mine in Rupovo Brdo, and they were not allowing miners to go to work. Mixed patrols were started by the villagers of Zaklopaca as both the Muslims and the Serbs were afraid; however, both Muslims and Serbian neighbours continued to socialise with each other. On 16th of May, 1992, Bozidar Trisic noticed three soldiers in the village who he did not recognise. He spoke to them and they said they were looking for Turks in the village. He informed them that there were no Turks in the village and that they could turn back. As the soldiers left, shooting could be heard in Gornja Zaklopaca part of the village. As he returned home, Bozidar Trisic noticed bullets landing in the village. Everyone in the village was very confused as no one knew whether the village was being attacked by Muslims or Serbs. Bozidar Trisic noticed that there was shooting from Serbian houses in the direction of an attack in the woods. He also saw unfamiliar soldiers who were firing at the village. The shooting lasted for 10 to 15 minutes, and soon after it finished the inhabitants of Zaklopaca noticed a convoy of passengers, vehicles passing by. Bozidar Trisic did not notice any police or military vehicles in the convoy. A number of villagers were killed in this attack, and following this the Muslim inhabitants left Zaklopaca and moved to Gerovi, a Muslim village. Following this, the Serb residents patrolled the village guarding both the Muslims and Serb houses. The Serb residents assisted their Muslim neighbours, providing them with food and cigarettes and other goods. The incident that occurred on that day was not planned and both Serbs and Muslims were in a dangerous situation. Not a single house was set alight or destroyed in this incident. Nobody brought Muslims in from elsewhere and killed them in Zaklopaca, only residents were killed. Bozidar Trisic considers that this incident may well have been revenge for the killing of the three territorials outside the barricaded mine. And that is the summary, and at that moment I do not have questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Trisic, as you have noted, your evidence in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- start by asking you about a time in early May 1992 when you say that two buses arrived in Zaklopaca carrying about 200 Muslims from nearby villages, including Pomol. You're aware of the event I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: These were families?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And in this group there were men and women of all ages and children?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 7 you said: "When we asked them why they had come there, they said that they had fled because the Muslim forces wanted to mobilise them into a detachment in Djile. Since they did not want to be mobilised, they fled to us for protection." Now, you would agree that it sounds strange to hear that a group of Muslim families, including women and children and the elderly, would be fleeing their nearby villages due to the fear of being mobilised into a military unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, you know who Omer Selimovic is; right? He was another resident of Zaklopaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 24671, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What you're going to see on your screen in a moment is a witness statement that Mr. Selimovic gave to this Tribunal in 2000. He mentioned on page 4 - if we could go to e-court page 4, please - on the second paragraph I'll read to you what he said in his statement. He mentioned the same arrival of people that you did but he described it differently. He said: "One day a large number of displaced persons from the village of Pomol arrived at Zaklopaca. Each of our families took in some of the displaced persons and they told us what had happened to them. Pomol is some 10 kilometres away, and the people told us that a Serb tank had shelled them; their houses had been burned and destroyed, and that they had run to the woods to escape." Now, does this refresh your recollection as to why all those people came to Zaklopaca?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: In talking with the people who came, mixed guards organised by neighbours, Muslims and us Serbs, it is correct that those people were placed in the elementary school and that the rest of them were placed at private Muslim houses. I personally asked them -- first of all, we were glad that they came. They were peace-loving people and they came - they fled, of course - they said that there was some things happening around the bauxite mine, that there were barricades, that a terrain was being cleared, and that they came there to get out of the chaos and to seek shelter for the time being. They told me personally that that is what they did. As for whether they fled or if they did not flee, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that they never told you that their village had been burned and that they were fleeing an attack from a Serb tank?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I did not ask them whether their village was burned. We did not ask them if the village was burned. They just told us that they came because they were supposed to be mobilised. It was a large number of citizens. They were supposed to be mobilised in the Djile detachment and so they came to seek temporary shelter. That's what they told me, at least. I mean, these were very, very nice people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the events of the 16th of May, 1992. I'm just going to start by asking you to verify a couple of basic points about the events of that day. First of all, over 60 of your neighbours from the village were killed that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And all of the victims were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: They were killed by gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you saw soldiers firing on the village that day?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll get to that. It's true that on that day you attended a barbecue at the house of your neighbour, Seban Selimovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And in the afternoon while you were on your way to a neighbour's shop you stopped to talk with your neighbour, Branko Julevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No, not the next day. The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. The same day you were speaking to your neighbour, Branko Julevic, and during that conversation three soldiers who you did not recognise approached --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Jolovic is the name, Branko Jolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification for the transcript. During that conversation it's true that three soldiers whom you did not recognise approached you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: They were in camouflage uniforms and were armed with automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: They were not in camouflage uniforms. They were in olive-green-grey uniforms and had automatic rifles, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So at paragraph 12 of your statement where you say, "They were in camouflage uniforms and had automatic rifles on their shoulders ..." that should be corrected; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, according to you, they said they were looking for Turks; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you understood these soldiers to be Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And this was the first sign to you that day that indicated that something was wrong; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And before the soldiers appeared, when you were talking to your neighbour, Mr. Jolovic, was he armed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I did not notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, if he were carrying, for example, a semi-automatic machine-gun, you would have noticed; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Certainly, of course I would have noticed. It's not something you can hide under a coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you are certain that your neighbour, Mr. Jolovic, did not approach you along with the other soldiers as a group; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No, sir. He was sitting outside of Vujadin Vasiljevic's house on a stump, on a tree stump, where wood is cut. He and Vujadin were sitting there and talking. At that moment I came by, walking from the shop. I stopped to talk to them for a while, just asking: How are you, et cetera, officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 24682, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: While that's coming up, you know who Semsudin Muskic is; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Muskic, Semsudin Muskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I take it you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: He was at the same barbecue you were attending that day?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, he and his brother with their entire families were sitting there in the yard. He had come a bit earlier. First he went to Vlasenica, then came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. He gave a statement on the 26th of June, 1998, to an examining judge of the cantonal court in Tuzla in connection with the investigation of Milenko Djuric and others for genocide committed in Zaklopaca. And what you have in front of you is a copy of his statement. I'd like to direct your attention to the bottom of page 1 in B/C/S and the top half of page 2 in the English. And what you'll see in the statement is he describes spending the whole day with his brother, Mevlo, in their neighbour Saban Selimovic's yard where there was a barbecue. And then in the lower half of English page 2 and the top of page 2 of the B/C/S he says: "At Saban's house we were joined for the rest of the day by our neighbour, Trisic Bozidar, a registrar. At about 16.55 I decided to go to my house which was about 20 metres away. I remember immediately turning on the TV as I entered my house, and at the time shown on the screen was 17.00. At that moment my brother Mevlo's children said some soldiers were coming, so I immediately went outside to see what kind of soldiers they were. That was when I saw four unidentified persons stepping out of a Honda passenger vehicle carrying automatic rifles and wearing the former JNA olive-grey uniform. I saw and recognised our neighbour Jolovic Brano, son of Radomir, accompanying the four men. Brano was carrying an M72 semi-automatic machine-gun. They were heading straight for Saban Selimovic's house. Outside the yard they were greeted by Trisic Bozo, the registrar. He spoke to them about something. I saw Bozidar trying to prevent them from going into the yard and I heard them shouting at him. Next, Trisic Bozidar made a hand sign to the rest of us who were observing the whole thing to flee. We realised the situation was critical and we all fled the house ..." He then goes on to describe automatic fire being opened a few minutes later. Now, from this statement it sounds like you by trying to prevent these armed men from going into your neighbour's house and signalling that there was danger, you might have saved this man's life. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, except that in this version where he says they attempted to go into the house of Saban Selimovic, that house was next door to mine, and I stopped these soldiers some 50 metres away from going into Vujadin Vasiljevic's house when they had crossed the river coming from the side of the main road. So it's true I saved not only his life but the lives of many Serbs and all the Muslims there. And of course I risked my own life, and I'm not sorry to have done it, in fact. I'm very glad I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So this statement also describes Brano Jolovic as being part of the group of soldiers approaching your area, and does this refresh your recollection as to what your neighbour, Mr. Jolovic, was doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: My neighbour, Mr. Jolovic, worked in the bauxite mines. In fact, he was a guard at the football stadium Milici --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not interested in the background about Mr. Jolovic. I'm just wondering if this refreshes your recollection as to what he was doing at that precise time.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I found my neighbours Jolovic and Vasiljevic sitting on the tree stump outside of Vujadin Vasiljevic's house. At some five minutes later, those three soldiers appeared. That's what I know. That's what I'm sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Now what he had come with, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. You went home to get dressed and to get your M48 rifle and you say that when you came out into your courtyard again you saw a soldier who had put a machine-gun on the water-pipes and was shooting at the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, except that when those three soldiers came back, they turned around immediately, one of them tried to take his rifle off, the other one jerked him away, and they returned to the road. A few minutes later in the upper village, Gornji Selo, shooting started, then I returned to Vujadin's house, took the house, and as I was approaching the house, not from the fountain but from the water-supply pipe, because there's a water-supply pipe from Zaklopaca to Milici and our city supply system, and between my house and Saban's house --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: -- bullets were whizzing and there was a cloud of dust --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm sorry to interrupt, but your statement is already in evidence so you don't have to repeat everything that's in there. I'd like you to just answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So you answered "yes" to my question about whether you saw a soldier shooting at the village. You previously, a few minutes ago, said when I asked you whether you saw soldiers shooting that day you said "no." So I take it you wish to correct that answer?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I saw a soldier shooting from that water-supply pipe, if you understand me --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: -- I didn't see the other soldiers shooting in Gornje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: He was on your property at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: You mean the soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: He was not on my estate. He was in front. He was in front of it, perhaps 50 to 100 metres outside my farm, just below the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. And you yelled at him to stop shooting and he did stop shooting, he left, and he did not turn to fire at you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, you were not out patrolling the village or participating in any of this shooting; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You stayed in your house during this time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You did not live in the centre of the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I lived closer to the entrance to the village, at least that part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you did not see what was happening in the centre of the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I did not see what was happening in the upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you had a Muslim neighbour named Adem Selimovic who went into the village to see what happened, and he came back a half-hour later and told you that there were many dead; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And at that point you went to your Muslim neighbours' houses and you told them that it would be best if they left the village and went to a place where only Muslims lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you said this -- pardon me. You said this because you knew that it wasn't safe for Muslims there; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And afterwards you went on a patrol of the village with other Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No. I went alone to see what happened with them. I saw they were missing. They were not there. And then I went further up the village where the Serb houses are and the house of Adem Selimovic and that's where I found them, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So it's true that afterwards you must have seen dozens of Muslims who had been your neighbours who had been shot to death at that point?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see him because that's in the upper part of the village and we were in the lower part of the village. In my part of the village, nobody was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So just to clarify, are you saying you never went to the upper part of the village after the incident to see what had happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No, I never went.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, ultimately all of your Muslim neighbours who were still alive moved out of Zaklopaca; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Things were still bad, but they returned and we saw each other almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But they did not return to live there. They returned to collect some of their belongings; that's right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, I noticed in your statement that you mentioned that not a single house was either set alight or destroyed during this incident, but it's true that Serbs ultimately moved into the houses that were previously owned by Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Muslim women who survived the massacre walked to Vlasenica, where they surrendered to Serb soldiers and were brought to the municipality building where they were required to sign away their houses and property to the Serbs, at which point they were bussed out of town in the direction of Kladanj. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the citation for that is Exhibit P418.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay, you said in paragraph 26 of your statement: "I was told there were claims that the attack on Zaklopaca was carried out by the Milici police station, or rather, its policemen, and that Rade Bjelanovic was the chief of the station. I state that this is not true because I would have recognised the policemen from the Milici police station who wore blue uniforms at the time."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, Mesudina Zaimhadzic was a resident of Zaklopaca who gave evidence here. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: She specifically identified a policeman whom she knew from Milici named Milomir Milosevic as a participant in the attack. Did you see Milomir Milosevic in Zaklopaca during the killings?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: She also said that at 5.00 p.m. she looked out the window of her house and saw about four or five army vehicles and one police car arriving. Do you not recall seeing a police car?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I do not recall and I did not see that. I didn't see a single police or military vehicle that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with the following four survivors of the Zaklopaca attack: Ibro Hamidovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Hakija and Havo Berbic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And Mersida Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: These people all gave statements under oath in 1995 to a magistrate in Tuzla, similar to the 1998 statement that we saw earlier from Semsudin Muskic. I want to quickly show you something from each of their statements, then I'm going to ask you a question about it. So could we have 65 ter number 64 -- sorry, 24678, please. This is going to be the statement of Ibro Hamidovic. And when it comes up, if we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. At the top of both pages what you'll see is that Mr. Hamidovic says: "On that very day, May 16th, 1992, about 4.00 p.m. I was in my house in the village of Zaklopaca. I suddenly saw three-four, no 7-8 vehicles pass through the village near my house, and the first of them was a police car. I recognised Milosevic Milomir, policeman, in the police car ..." And then it goes on to describe gun-fire being opened shortly thereafter. In the interests of time, I'm not going to go through the other three statements of Havo Berbic and Hakija Berbic and Mersida Salihovic, but I'll just tell you that all three of them also in their statements recall seeing at least one police car. So what I'm wondering is whether it's possible that you just didn't see a police car or police cars that were actually in Zaklopaca that day?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I did not see that car. I did not see any police cars. Only in the upper part, the first 100, 200 metres into the upper village. The police was changing the local water-supply pipes and police patrols were taking turns around the water-pipes. Milosevic was a policeman, but that day I didn't see him. I did not see any police cars that day, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But you acknowledge --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: It's possible that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I kindly ask the Prosecutor to tell us where it is stated that the police car was in the village, because here it says it passed through the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can take up that issue. But, Mr. Trisic, what -- did you try to say something? It's possible ... and it was -- and you were cut off. What did you try to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that police cars drove up to the water-supply pipe and that they were noticed because there was a police patrol at the water installation every day; it was guarded by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And what you're saying is that could have happened without you personally seeing it; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not see any police cars or military vehicles that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. My last few questions I'd like to ask you about some statements that you make in your witness statement. At paragraph 23 you say that the attack on Zaklopaca happened spontaneously and it had not been planned, and then at paragraph 27 of your statement you give your opinion as to what motivated the attackers. You say: "A convoy of JNA military vehicles was travelling through Milici that day withdrawing towards Serbia and they encountered many problems on their way. It was probably one of those people who, in revenge for the killing of the three territorials, asked someone where they could find Muslims close by, and a group of them and the volunteers who were in Milici at that time went to Zaklopaca and caused this incident." Now, this statement is just a guess, right? Because you just testified that you didn't know who these attackers were?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you think you can conclude your cross in ten minutes? I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant re-examination. Then please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trisic, on page 55 of today's LiveNote, you were asked whether it was strange, now I'll give you the exact quotation in English: [In English] "Now, you would agree that it sounds strange to hear that a group of Muslim families, including women and children and the elderly, would be fleeing their nearby village due to the fear of being mobilised into a military unit; correct?" [Interpretation] And you said "yes." Now, did you agree with that being strange?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that that was strange. It wasn't strange because everybody avoided mobilisation, Serb and Muslim people alike. And of course everybody's going to try to get away from that hell that was going on up there, how should I know, around Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today on page 59 the question implied that that was the first sign that something went wrong, when these three soldiers showed up. When did you find out about the ambush when these three persons were killed beforehand, when they were killed by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I found out only on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On pages 61 and 62 you said that you heard that shooting had started in the upper part of the village. All of those who entered the village then, who got into the village, did they have to pass by you on that bridge?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: They didn't have to. They could also enter along the road that led to Gornji Zalukovi [phoen] from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 65 you briefly said "yes" in response to the Prosecutor's question whether Serbs moved into Muslim houses. Can you tell us who these Serbs were that moved into Muslim houses and on which basis?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Serbs who moved into Muslim houses in Zaklopaca were from the area of Rupovo Brdo because they had been expelled from there by the Muslim population Brdo and Slivovo, and then they fled to Zaklopaca and moved into Muslim houses in Zaklopaca. There were people from Gornje Vrsinje too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These houses, were they handed over to them, were they given to them as a gift?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No, they were not given to them as a gift. They just lived there and they really did take care of the houses properly. Afterwards, the houses were returned to the Muslims and then now they renovated these houses, whereas these people moved back to their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is not reflected here, whether they became the owners of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: No, they did not become the owners of that because that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also it was mentioned that certain certificates were asked for in terms of them giving houses as gifts. How many cases were there of having ownership changed in Vlasenica in terms of property being taken away from someone?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I don't know of a single case of somebody's property being seized from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Tomo Savkic, Milenko Stanic, and other representatives of the Serb community in the authorities in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they participate or contribute in any way to this incident in Zaklopaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that as going beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, it had been implied that police vehicles had been noticed there and the police is part of the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it necessarily arose from the cross-examination. You could have raised it in your direct examination. I tend to agree with the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Robinson, would you like to help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the Prosecution's cross-examination called into question who it was who was responsible for these killings, and that it goes directly to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, you said today that you did not recognise these people and in some statement that was read out too, that these people who were shooting had not been recognised. Now, this is what I'm interested in: To the best of your knowledge, the police of Vlasenica or Milici, did it take part in this and what was the attitude of the authorities in Milici and Vlasenica vis-a-vis that incident?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I think that the authorities did not know about this incident because every effort was made to go on living together so that we'd continue living together as we had before that. So I deny that the authorities knew about this incident at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the possibility of police presence in securing the waterworks. Did you know that police vehicles could follow the military column through those municipalities? I'd like to read this out to you, this statement of Zoran Durmic who testified here only recently. Paragraph 8, Zoran Durmic's statement. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "We were stopped at the roadblock and we were asked where we were going and we said we were escorting the military column to Zvornik. All of those who were at the barricade were stern and unpleasant and they said" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's too fast. Take a look at the transcript and begin from there again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would object to this as being a very leading line of questioning, essentially using the words of another witness to suggest something relating to this roadblock and the military column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you, Mr. File. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Just put your question not in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: What were all the ways in which a police vehicle could have been seen without it being involved in --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I withdraw it. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Trisic: You did not recognise it. Did you hear from anyone else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your last question? We need to rise. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, you said that you did not recognise any of those soldiers. Did you hear from anyone, from any of the other locals, about them having recognised those persons who stopped there and opened fire?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: I did not hear any such thing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question. Where were these people killed? Where were they, in houses or what? How come so many people were killed in 10 or 15 minutes only?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: That's what the locals told me, that people were killed as they were fleeing from their homes, as they were trying to save themselves in the woods, in the river valley, et cetera. All of those who stayed behind, in their homes, had not been touched. Nothing happened to them. Ibro Hamidovic and Semsudin at least said that when he came to see me in Vlasenica three days later, he and his wife and their sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trisic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR TRISIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trisic. I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll -- today, just for today, the Chamber is minded to take an hour break for lunch and adjourn at 3.00 unless it causes problem to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.42 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Could -- yes, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I forget to mention that we'll proceed for this session pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Morrison being away. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, did you give my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that you already know that we need to pause between question and answer, and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 1D07815.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the first page, it is the statement that I read and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show President Bulatovic the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic. I'm not sure whether I heard you or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't have mike. It was functioning until recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you try it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Now I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. It was my notebook, thank you, that pushed the priority button. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would the answers to those questions basically be the same like those contained in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same but I must note that I can give additional argumentation to this honourable Trial Chamber, including facts that could not be included in the first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, can I please tender this 92 ter package now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In addition, for President Bulatovic we have eight associated exhibits, two of which were not on our 65 ter list, which are the last two in our chart, and we would ask that they be added as they came up during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as regards the areas the witness wanted to add would be led live by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I think if there's additional explanations required, we will elicit those in re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Any objections, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, but I just wanted to clarify. In relation to the contemporaneous records that are basically addressed by the witness in the statement, it's my understanding that they are tendered in full and not just one page. Is that understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to raise that, if you do not raise it. As regards the four, one, two, three, four stenographic notes, I take it you're tendering only those pages shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, if there's no objection by the Prosecution, we would like to have the whole -- those particular ones admitted. But if this -- if the Prosecution would only want those pages then we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, then I would like to turn to you and would like to hear from you --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- why they should be admitted in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, actually I join the request by the Defence that they should be admitted in their entirety, in particular 65 ter 06141. It's -- the entire -- the entire document refers to the stances taken by the peace negotiations and they are actually of interest for all. It should be -- it should be in full. In particular, the Prosecution also will use this document to highlight certain passages, and it is very difficult to just have it piecemeal because it's all the time about these negotiations. Therefore I think it's useful to the Court to have it in full. In relation to the three SDC minutes, there are, at least in 06243 and 06256, a few passages in there that are not really related to Bosnia, but rather to the financing of the VJ. But there are -- it's not many. So mostly these -- the discussions are related to problems in the territory of Republika Srpska, the co-operation of the leaderships and the armies, and I think it should be also before the Court in full. And in relation to 06253, it is also entirely about negotiations and the outcome of the negotiations, the positions taken by the Bosnian Serbs and other participants; therefore, I think to have them in full would assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given the circumstances, we'll admit them all in their entirety. Shall we give the numbers for the statement as well as the other associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the 92 ter statement, 65 ter 1D7815 will be Exhibit D3051, and the eight associated exhibits will be assigned Exhibits D3052 through Exhibits D3059 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read the summary of President Bulatovic's statement which has now been admitted. I'll be reading it in English. [In English] Momir Bulatovic served as President of Montenegro from 23rd of December, 1990, to the 15th of January, 1998. He was prime minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 19th of May, 1998, to 4th of November, 2000. President Bulatovic believes that the Bosnian Serbs, led by Radovan Karadzic, did not need nor want the war. They favoured the status quo of remaining in Yugoslavia. Everything they did was in response to acts and threats of the Bosnian Muslims which were determined to rule over all of Bosnia. President Bulatovic is convinced that the war could have been avoided in March 1992 had the Bosnian Muslims agreed to the Cutileiro Plan. However, they were persuaded by the Americans that they could get a lot more if they rejected the plan. More than three years and thousands of lives later, they ended up with the Dayton Agreement which was almost identical to the Cutileiro Plan. On September the 16th, 1991, President Bulatovic attended a meeting of high representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina in Belgrade. The meeting was called for the purpose of finding solutions to preserve Yugoslavia. Dr. Karadzic and Adil Zulfikarpasic, a Muslim leader, were invited to attend as special guests after they had concluded the Serb-Muslim historic agreement, calling for a peaceful sharing of power in Bosnia. President Alija Izetbegovic chose not to attend this meeting. When it became inevitable that Bosnia would not remain in Yugoslavia, Dr. Karadzic favoured a separate Bosnian Serb entity in which the Serbs would be able to govern themselves politically, rather than being under the political control of the Bosnian Muslims. Dr. Karadzic always expressed the wish that Muslims and Croats would live in the Serb entity with full respect for their rights, while Serbs who preferred to live in the Bosnian Muslim or Croat entity would be free to do so and to have their rights respected. This was the principle behind the Cutileiro Plan to which Dr. Karadzic agreed in March 1992 and which he supported both privately and publicly. President Izetbegovic [sic] never heard Dr. Karadzic saying anything that would lead him to believe that he favoured the expulsion of Muslims and Croats from the Serb areas of Bosnia. He was not aware of any joint criminal enterprise among leaders of the Bosnian Serbs and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to expel Muslims and Croats from the Serb areas in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Line 3 should have read "President Bulatovic." Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I hope I didn't say that. President Bulatovic I said, but somebody -- I don't know how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said so. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: President Bulatovic is familiar with the strategic goals endorsed by the Bosnian Serb Assembly in May 1992. He never understood the goal of separation to mean physical separation of ethnic or religious groups through expulsions. He always understood it to be in the political sense so that Serbs would be able to govern themselves rather than being out-voted by the Muslims. President Bulatovic is aware that during the war in Bosnia, members of the population of all ethnic groups suffered expulsions. He does not believe that this resulted from these policy of Radovan Karadzic. Instead, it resulted from the collective mentality of the population, who reacted instinctively when war broke out because of what they had experienced in the Second World War, when the Ustashas, aided by the Muslims, killed many Serb civilians in villages throughout Bosnia. When the war broke out in Bosnia, it was impossible for Dr. Karadzic or any other political leader to control the population to prevent such crimes. President Bulatovic had many conversations with Dr. Karadzic about the shelling of Sarajevo. Dr. Karadzic recognised the political liability and damage that the shelling did to the cause of Bosnian Serbs in the eye of the world. He told President Bulatovic that when he had inquired of General Mladic and the Bosnian Serb army whether the shelling could be stopped, he was told that the shelling was necessary to avoid the Serb positions being overrun by the Bosnian Muslim army, which would then attack Serb civilians in the suburbs of Sarajevo. Dr. Karadzic and President Bulatovic also discussed allegations frequently made by international negotiators that the shelling was not limited to repulsing military attacks but was aimed at the civilian areas. Dr. Karadzic told him that he had banned shelling of civilian areas on a number of occasions and had done everything he could to prevent the unnecessary or disproportionate shelling of Sarajevo. The shelling of the Markale Market in Sarajevo on 5th of February, 1994, was discussed at the Supreme Defence Council meeting on 7th of February, 1994. General Perisic, the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav national army, said: "Over there in Republika Srpska they say that they are certainly not the ones who did it, and the likelihood is small." Perisic went on to report that: "Our military experts claim that this is impossible. We assume that the same was done in Vase Miskina Street - that the explosive was prepared ahead of time and placed in a number of spots and that at a given moment the signal was given to set it off when the largest number of people were there." In August 1992, the issue of detention camps in BH came to the forefront of negotiations after the news media wrote about those camps. When reports of mistreatment of persons in those camps surfaced, he discussed this with Radovan Karadzic. Dr. Karadzic appeared to be surprised at the mistreatment. He told President Bulatovic that he had guarantees that the refugees in the camps would be taken care of and treated according to the Geneva Conventions. President Bulatovic spoke with Radovan Karadzic about the issue of paramilitaries. Dr. Karadzic didn't want the paramilitary groups in Bosnia and they caused great problems for the local Bosnian Serb authorities and the Serb citizens, as well Dr. Karadzic wanted to get rid of those people but simply didn't have the ability to do it. In 1994, President Bulatovic became aware that a rift had developed between President Karadzic and General Mladic. During sessions of the Supreme Defence Council in 1994, which is a body of Yugoslav defence system, they approved some personnel actions designed to pension off generals who were believed to support President Karadzic, such as General Stanislav Galic. In a discussion on 11th of July, 1994, they were told that General Mladic had proposed pensioning some generals who had "turned to the Karadzic option." As the war went on, President Karadzic lost a lot of his political power. General Mladic had become an icon, and the Bosnian Serb Assembly was dominated by the representatives of the people who were manning the trenches and who were against all forms of compromise. At one point it seemed that President Karadzic had lost control over General Mladic and the VRS. President Bulatovic got to know Radovan Karadzic quite well over the years 1991-1997. He never heard him express any hatred for Muslims or Croats or saying anything which would lead him to believe that Dr. Karadzic was in favour of crimes committed against people from those groups. He can say with absolute certainty that Radovan Karadzic would never have been in favour of executing prisoners, whether in Srebrenica or anywhere else. President Bulatovic was present during negotiations in Belgrade in July 1996 when United States' diplomat Richard Holbrooke came to Belgrade to negotiate for the resignation of Radovan Karadzic as part of the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement. He personally heard Richard Holbrooke say that he had the guarantee of the United States president that Karadzic would not prosecuted by The Hague Tribunal if he resigns and withdrew from politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems that the interpreters took part of your summary so they didn't interpret your last words. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. [In English] President Bulatovic was present during negotiations in Belgrade in July 1996 when United States' diplomat Richard Holbrooke came to Belgrade to negotiate for the resignation of Radovan Karadzic as part of the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement. President Bulatovic personally heard Richard Holbrooke say that he had the guarantee of the United States president that Karadzic would not be prosecuted at The Hague Tribunal if he resigned and withdrew from politics. And what probably was not caught was that I said that this is summary and I don't have any questions for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. Bulatovic, as you have noted, your evidence in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had actually expected that one or two documents would be addressed viva voce, but that's obviously not happening. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, in your statement, paragraphs 24 through to 26, you referred to the shelling of Sarajevo, and in this context you referred to the shorthand notes from the session of the council of co-ordination of state policy held on 18th August 1992. To you and Milan Panic and the others present, Mr. Karadzic would say that he was not in control of the guns and parts of the VRS and they acted on their own; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The question is too broad. I'm not sure exactly what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was asking you whether Mr. Karadzic when -- when addressed on certain events during meetings, he would say that he was not in control of the guns - for instance, the ones in Sarajevo - and he were not -- and certain parts of the VRS acted on their own. Isn't that what he at times would say to either you or other people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether the stenogram faithfully reflects the discussion, yes, I confirm that it does. And if I understand your question correctly, it was not just on that occasion but on numerous other occasion that we faced the fact that there was a civil war in Bosnia and that it was not possible to establish control and command over each individual unit. I don't believe that General Mladic could have done that either and especially not the political leader who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, when you say these kind of things, you rely on claims that the -- that Mr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership basically put forward to you in such discussions; right? You were not yourself there to make your own observations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you permit me, my source of information was not just from contacts with Mr. Karadzic. At that time there was a conference on the former Yugoslavia, the section for Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were international mediators. At the time Lord Owen had a leading role together with Cyrus Vance, and then after he left that post we had Mr. Stoltenberg. Numerous times in Geneva while we were trying to find a peaceful solution we faced the fact that shelling was going on. We sought confirmation also from independent organs. We wanted the shelling to stop, thus we did not just have to believe one side. But according to UN sources as well and those of the observer missions it was evident that the shelling of Sarajevo was going on outside of any kind of logic or plan. This did not cause only us to be concerned but also the peace mediators. We remember the sincere --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- horror by Lord Owen -- from Lord Owen particularly --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. The Chamber will rise for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. --- Break taken at 2.19 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For record, we are now sitting in full Bench. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I had interrupted you because we have only very little time here and I hadn't asked you about the negotiations with the internationals and what they told you. So I would rather prefer that you stick and answer questions very precisely and the exact question asked. Let me put to you, you yourself, you noticed during meetings or negotiations with Mr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership that when they were under pressure they sometimes turned to political manoeuvring and even told the truth. Did you notice that -- untruth, sorry, the untruth. Did you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to answer your questions with the best intention. I didn't mean to give a broader answer. But I'm just saying that at the peace negotiations these precisely were the topics: The shelling of Sarajevo. The shells were being counted and it was not something that only we did; the entire conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina was doing that and it was also the UN monitoring system that was doing that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you again. My question was whether you in your dealings with Mr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders noticed that at times they were telling the untruth or resorted to political manoeuvring. That was the question, and it's actually you either did or you did not.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But I am experiencing that as a leading question. I would be very grateful if you would help me by telling me what was the sense of that, is anybody speaking the truth or not in a situation when a city was being shelled and when lives were being lost and considerable damage was being inflicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I personally cannot put these things together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you again. The Prosecution is entitled to ask leading questions and that's what I'm doing, and I was actually hoping you had answered the question but you didn't. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think witness was confused with the -- with your previous question. The question was whether Mr. Karadzic and other Bosnian Serb leaders at times were telling you or the other -- or other representative telling untruth? That's a general question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information, I don't think so. I believed what they were saying and the reason that I did so was that other information and other sources confirmed such a state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please have 65 ter 24596B in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up it's a part of your book: "Rules of Silence," in which you describe the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and your observations. And this particular part here of the book refers to your description of an event that took place in Geneva on the night of the 19th of January, 1994. I don't -- yeah. Yes. You describe here in this -- on this page you describe here your negotiations between the Serb and the Croat side and an agreement was reached on a Serb proposal of an interethnic demarcation map and that the next step to be taken was that cartographers from both sides were preparing a detailed map that would take into account the Croatian territorial request. You remember this situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I remember it very well. I'm the author of the book. Of course I re-read it and I think that it faithfully reflects the events at the time and how I experienced them. But if you permit me, I am saying something else here than what you are putting to me in the question from a little bit earlier. It wasn't the cartographers who were supposed to determine the borders. It clearly states here that they tried, President Karadzic and other members of the Serbian delegation, to get the territory of 17.5 per cent which would satisfy the demands of the Croatian President Tudjman in the sense of the possibility of signing an historic agreement on co-operation between Serbs and Croats. This passage for me and as well as in another incident are an illustration of tragic fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the major responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- of their political representatives. If you look carefully --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you. What I was actually referring to is that the remaining step to make is prepare the maps that everybody had agreed upon, and that is actually described here on this page. And you describe also on this page that Radovan Karadzic said that there was no need for them, the cartographers, to work together and that the whole job was going to be completed by the Republika Srpska experts. And then you say: "I believe that Tudjman was not really closed the door behind him when Radovan Karadzic asked: 'Does anyone have an eraser?' Milosevic and I could not believe that he was going to erase the line that they had just agreed on ..." That is what the situation was at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Obviously we are reading the same text in two different ways. I'm describing here the drama that is supposed to result in the drawing of maps. It says that one move on the 1:50.000 map with a pencil is drawing a line on a territory that is soaked with blood and suffering. This is obviously an honest attempt, but it's also obvious that this war that was tearing up Bosnia and Herzegovina with casualties and victims on all sides made it impossible to make a compromise. It's not about speaking the truth or lying here --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- it's about being able to withstand the burden of loss of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I mean, I just read to you your own words that you have written in the book and we can see that here in both languages. Do you deny that it was like this, how you describe it in the book, that Radovan Karadzic as soon as Tudjman was out of the door erased the line that they just had agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now I don't understand what you're saying, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I simply read to you what you had written in your book, and I assumed that what you had written here is your observation at the time and it had been like you had written it here.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying any of what is written here, but I cannot agree with your interpretation of one sentence, that you have the right to put to me as the Office of the Prosecutor. You can interrupt me even now, but I don't see in this sentence what you are suggesting. This is not a story about a liar who is erasing things from an agreement. This is a long story. There are many pages before and many pages after that show with what difficulty, how arduously we were trying to reach peace in Bosnia. I cannot agree with you interpretation that this text shows me depicting Radovan Karadzic as a liar. It may be your interpretation, but I cannot agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 24596A displayed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it is another part of your book and it is an excerpt that deals with the negotiations on the Vance-Owen Plan in 1993 and it is quite a number of pages, but on the first page and the second paragraph you state that: The Yugoslav side truly wanted peace and were ready to make any reasonable compromise in order to achieve it. And, Mr. Bulatovic, the reasonable compromise that you actually had seen in the Vance-Owen Plan in 1993, the Bosnian Serb leadership and Mr. Karadzic did not share your -- this view, that it is a reasonable compromise; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also say here your own assessment that the Vance -- it was your own assessment that the Vance-Owen Plan would protect the interest of the Bosnian Serbs, end the war, and set a legal procedure for resolving the remaining disputed issues; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct with the proviso that I personally supported every peace plan, beginning with the Lord Carrington plan and ending with the Dayton Accords, because I believed and I still believe that a bad peace plan is still better than a good war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as I read in your book, and we can move on to the second page in both languages, that you and Mr. Milosevic did all you could to convince the Bosnian Serb leaders to accept the plan. And when they left in the evening, you actually understood that they had accepted it and were finally agreeing to it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we look at the last paragraph in the B/C/S and also in the English. But immediately afterwards, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik broke their promise and they declared to be opposed to the agreement. That is how it is described in your book. Is that also your recollection now?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is said in the book that the MPs who were supposed to make their decision were warriors. I'm very sorry that plan failed. Together with the then-Greek Prime Minister Mitsotakis, President Milosevic, I invested a lot of effort for that peace plan to succeed, but we failed unfortunately. But I don't think it was a game played by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of Republika Srpska. I believe it was a kind of madness that reigned in their parliament at the time and all of that is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not -- I'm just going a little bit further in the text. You also describe here that you had been following this in Athens, further negotiations involving the Greek Prime Minister Mitsotakis, and at that time you -- it ended with Mr. Karadzic signing and provisionally accepting the plan. And it also refers here to the fact that you, Mr. Milosevic, and Prime Minister Mitsotakis attended then the RS Assembly Session that followed in which the signature was not ratified; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move further to page 4 in both languages and it's the third paragraph in the English and the last paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You describe here what was going on on this Assembly session and you state in the book Mr. Karadzic did not support the plan as you, and obviously the other participants of the delegation from Belgrade had expected but rather spoke to the contrary. That is what happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The book reflects my impression that I still hold today, that President Karadzic, cunningly and in a veiled way was a man under great pressure and against signing that plan. I know that it was against his convictions, against his deep beliefs, but we exerted so much pressure on him in Athens that he accepted to inform in a skilful political way his own Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you -- further in your book you describe how after the speeches that you, the delegation, from Belgrade, in particular Mr. Milosevic, gave, the atmosphere changed and you had basically the hope that the plan was -- would be accepted. And then there was a break for a caucuses meeting. And then -- now I want to quote to you - it's from page 5 in the English and it's the same page in the B/C/S - you say: "The good opportunity for peace got lost because the session was interrupted for a caucuses meeting to which you had no access and you call it political manoeuvring so that the plan was not accepted."
