Is that a correct description of what you felt at the time, that you were outmanoeuvred on purpose?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You could say that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also described further in your book that the same repeated itself with the Contact Group plan in 1994, and here you say in relation to July 1994 you say: "Even this time we were assured that the decision on the peace plan would be positive. The difference this time was that we had more reserve towards the sincerity of the RS leadership's intentions." Is that also how you felt about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, if it is coming from a same -- but why don't we add this part to the previous exhibit instead of giving a separate number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have no objections. Only we gave it a separate number because we felt it would maybe be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add that part to the previous exhibit, i.e., Exhibit P6159.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now please have 65 ter 24585 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a transcript of the raw materials gathered by the BBC for their video: "Death of Yugoslavia." It has disappeared. Okay. Thank you. You remember that you took part in this series of interviews that were conducted on the "Death of Yugoslavia" with quite a number of protagonists?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this as well as I remember regretting it. It's the kind of journalism where you talk for two hours and somebody cuts out five minutes from that, the bit that suits them. Let me just look at this text which is in front of me in English, which is not a problem, but I'd just like to see when this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is actually to me also not clear when this -- when you had these talks with a journalist, but it is the raw material. It's not the few minutes that were basically later on aired. It's the entire transcript of the talks and it's only identified on -- according to writers, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is a date at the very bottom. I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes, October -- 7 October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that match your own memory on when these talks took place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But the BBC series called "Death of Yugoslavia" was filmed and broadcast after 2000. That's why this date in 1994 confuses me. That time when I talked to the BBC was after I stopped my involvement in politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also cannot clarify this now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you remember it was in 2000 or when did you stop?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this text, it's the BBC story about the death of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and logically this refers to the communist party of Yugoslavia, because in 1994 there were other, more important topics than the central committee and the 14th Congress of the party which was in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me perhaps clarify something. This is quite an extensive transcript, and according to this transcript you addressed a lot of topics. And we are not concerned with these early topics that obviously were touched upon with the journalist, at least according to this. Let's move to page 28 and on this page you speak about an event that you may remember where there was the bombing of Gorazde in April 1994. And here we have -- we have here -- and it says here 8 October 1994. We have here the event that you yourself heard from the police that Gorazde was being bombarded. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now reading this, yes, I believe it's fairly reflected.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said here yourself you and Mr. Milosevic were stunned that such a stupid move could have been timed in such a way to destroy all diplomatic efforts invested before that and that you then confronted Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. You did that, did you -- didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you go through the document, I'll be able to confirm or deny. But I cannot see yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go to the next page, please. Here in the upper part you see basically how Mr. Milosevic and you were upset about what had happened and that you basically called them and that they first denied that they were attacking Gorazde, and when you confronted them with proof they said they would stop it. Do you remember that situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's say that's the way it was. Unfortunately there were many similar situations. This is an overture into the NATO bombing of the VRS positions that followed later. Yes, that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender the pages that I just referred to; that is, pages 28 and 29. I will also use another excerpt so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit these two pages. We'll add another --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- when you present it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have to go back to page 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- let's give the number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Page 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you describe here and tell the journalist the situation that we actually spoke about a bit earlier, namely, the talks you had with Mr. Karadzic in Belgrade the day before the Bijeljina Assembly session. And you mention here that you wrote a letter to Bijeljina and the key argument in the letter as it -- as you say here, "signed by Cosic, Milosevic, and me was that they had no right to decide on the fate of all of us, especially when they are not as endangered as they had represented it to their own people." What you have mentioned here is -- did happen and you fought about that; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a period of great political divisions between the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the leadership of -- I just wanted to inform this Court that in that period Serbia and Montenegro were placed under very hard sanctions. We were not able to buy food or medicine for our babies and we felt our very existence was in danger. It was a completely different feeling than the feeling people in Bosnia and Herzegovina had. And here speaking of political differences, I cannot judge who was right and who was wrong. Our anxiety in Serbia and Montenegro was due to the fact that we were placed in unbearable living conditions. But still, we had peace, whereas over there there was war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender the pages 21 and 22 of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and that's all pages for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be added to P6160.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I will now refer to paragraph 20 of your statement where you say that all ethnic groups suffered expulsion and you also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that. Mr. Bulatovic, do you have your statement with you in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also state that this ethnic -- this expulsion was not the result of Mr. Karadzic's policy but rather resulted from the collective mentality of the population at that time and you refer to some details. Mr. Bulatovic, is it your evidence that the expulsion and crimes that the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims suffered during the period from 1991 through to 1995 in Croatia and in Bosnia are not the result of the policies and the actions of their respective leaderships? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very strong lifelong conviction is that it was a consequence of the civil war that raged in those areas, and that civil war was due to the uncontrolled and unlawful breakup of the previous state; that is to say the expulsions and the crimes are a consequence of the fact that there was a civil war not that there was any plan. I am proud - and I want to emphasise - that my country, Montenegro, was an open door to many people who found refuge there. 700.000 inhabitants of the country I'm proud to lead received 72.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, including 30 per cent Muslims. They found shelter in Montenegro and thanks to the United Nations -- of course you are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I interrupted here just because of time concerns. I fully understand that you wish to make this point clear, but unfortunately I have no time to do that. So -- but it's a bit not exactly answer my question, but let me put this to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue tomorrow, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask two more questions because then this is finished? But I can also do it tomorrow, whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is only two questions, then we can continue with the indulgence of the staff, interpreters and court reporter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, just so that it is finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you saying that the population, no matter what ethnicity, are expelling and killing each other on a mass scale in a huge territory because it's their mentality and because it's a war and not their leaderships or the people who are directing the armies?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, then I would say I don't believe there was a plan or that any side had a possibility, including Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, to order crimes and expulsions. I am sure and I know from the entire history of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the many decades of peaceful coexistence that when a war begins, when the earth moves under them, people are capable of crimes and they flee to territories where they feel safe. I cannot believe that there was a plan because I know Bosnia too well, its history, and its people. I talked to all of those people, including President Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, the Bosnian Croat leader. We spent many years together. I know President Karadzic very well. I would bet everything I earned in my life that these people were not criminals. They were in difficult positions in very difficult times, horrible times. And believe me, every 50 years in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff, such crimes and such expulsions repeat themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is -- that concludes this chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Bulatovic, we'll continue tomorrow. I'd like to advise you -- I think you understand English. I wanted to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
